Structure from Motion (SfM) methods have advanced to
the point where they can accurately estimate camera poses
even under moderately challenging conditions. However,

as a snapshot of the scene that can be matched against sub-
sequent images to compute relative camera poses. This as-
sumption, however, ignores the continuous nature of cam-
era motion and becomes especially problematic during fast
movements where motion blur can severely degrade ac-
curacy.

Since no existing dataset includes all the necessary data
to train such a model, we construct our own dataset using
a subset of ScanNet++v2 [47] and show how we obtain re-
alistic motion blur that allows for generalization to in-the-
wild images. Furthermore, the fully differentiable nature of
our method enables us to refine our model using real-world
motion-blurred images, even when ground-truth flows and
depths are not available for training. We evaluate our model
with angular and translational velocity estimates on real-
world motion blurred images to test the generalization ca-
pabilities of our model. Our method runs in real-time at 30
FPS and obtains significantly more accurate velocity esti-
mates compared to the existing state of the art methods.

**Structured Highlights for the Research Paper**

**Title**: Image_as_an_IMU_Estimating CAMer_a_Motion_from_a_Single_Motion-Blurred__Image_078869f1fccf1141

**Abstract**: The paper introduces a novel method for estimating camera motion using a single motion-blurred image. The approach leverages motion blur as a rich cue for camera pose estimation without treating it as an artifact. The method predicts a dense motion flow field and a monocular depth map directly from the blurred image, then recovers camera velocity using a linear least squares approach under the small motion assumption. The method outperforms existing techniques like MASt3R and COLMAP in angular and translational velocity estimation. The pipeline uses synthetic data from ScanNet++v2 and real motion-blurred images for training, achieving real-time performance at 30 FPS.

---

**Key Visual Findings**:
1. The method successfully recovers camera motion from a single blurred image, demonstrating the effectiveness of motion blur as a motion cue.
2. The recovered motion flow field and depth map provide accurate relative pose estimates, highlighting the robustness of the approach.
3. Real-time performance at 30 FPS is achieved, showing practical applicability.

---

**Experimental Setup and Validation**:
1. The method uses synthetic data from ScanNet++v2, augmented with realistic motion blur.
2. Real-world motion-blurred images are used to refine the model, ensuring generalization.
3. The pipeline is fully differentiable, enabling end-to-end training without ground-truth data for flow and depth.

---

**Core Innovation**:
A novel approach that directly estimates camera motion from a single blurred image by predicting a dense motion flow field and depth map, then recovering relative pose using a linear least squares method under the small motion assumption.

---

**Technical Approach**:
- Predicts dense motion flow and monocular depth map from a single image.
- Uses a linear least squares system to recover relative pose.
- The method is fully differentiable, allowing end-to-end training with real-world data.

---

**Quantitative Findings**:
1. Achieves state-of-the-art angular and translational velocity estimates.
2. Outperforms existing methods like MASt3R and COLMAP in accuracy.

---

**Limitations & Assumptions**:
1. Assumes small camera motion (valid for real-time applications).
2. Relies on synthetic data for training, potentially limiting generalization to other environments.
3. Performance may degrade under extreme motion blur or varying exposure times.

---

**Domain Impact**:
- The method is theoretically significant for real-time applications like robotics and VR/AR.
- Practically, it provides a robust solution for camera pose estimation in environments with fast camera movements, improving accuracy and reliability.
